questions.question_text: A ranger compares the number of nests found in forest, grassland, wetland and dunes. Which display is most suitable?

options.why: Joining habitat categories suggests continuous change between categories that have no time order.
A timeline places events in time, but these data compare habitat categories.
A number line locates values but does not compare named habitat frequencies.

questions.solution_text: The habitats are categories, so separate columns make their counts easy to compare.

questions.question_text: Scientists record a lake's depth on the first day of each month for a year. Which display best shows the changing depth?

options.why: Repeated symbols compare counts but do not show the month-to-month change clearly.
An unordered list removes the time sequence needed to see how depth changes.
One column can show only one value and cannot represent twelve monthly depths.

questions.solution_text: A line graph places the months in order and shows how depth changes across the year.

questions.question_text: Butterfly counts in four gardens are $12$, $20$, $28$ and $36$. Which picture-graph key gives whole symbols and a manageable number of symbols?

options.why: The counts are not all multiples of five, so several rows need fractional symbols.
The counts are not multiples of ten, producing awkward fractional symbols throughout.
This is exact but requires 96 symbols altogether, making the display crowded.

questions.solution_text:
$12\div4=3$, $20\div4=5$, $28\div4=7$, $36\div4=9$
The key of $4$ uses whole symbols without overcrowding.

questions.question_text: Native-bee counts at several sites range from $18$ to $67$. Which vertical scale is most sensible for a column graph starting at $0$?

options.why: This fits exactly but creates 67 intervals, making the axis unnecessarily crowded.
Only two large intervals make differences between site counts hard to judge.
This scale stops below the largest value of 67, so one column cannot fit.

questions.solution_text: A maximum of $70$ fits $67$, and steps of $10$ give seven equal, readable intervals.

questions.question_text: A graph will compare reptile counts at Rock, Sand, Creek and Scrub sites. Which axis plan is correct?

options.text: Reptile count horizontally; sites vertically with a number scale
options.why: This tries to place named site categories on a numerical vertical scale.
This provides no numerical axis on which to show each reptile count.
This leaves out the site categories that the counts must be compared across.

questions.solution_text: The category names belong on the horizontal axis and their frequencies on the vertical scale.

questions.question_text: A pond's dragonfly counts over six consecutive weeks are $24$, $31$, $29$, $38$, $42$ and $36$. Which display-and-scale plan is best?

options.text: Line graph; weeks equally spaced; vertical scale $0$–$45$ in steps of $5$
Column graph; counts as categories; vertical scale $0$–$45$ in steps of $5$
options.why: This treats the six numerical counts as category labels and hides their time sequence.

options.text: Line graph; weeks in any order; vertical scale $0$–$45$ in steps of $5$
options.why: A line graph needs chronological order; rearranged weeks would show a false pattern.

options.text: Line graph; weeks equally spaced; vertical scale $0$–$40$ in steps of $10$
options.why: This scale cannot show the largest count of 42 because it stops at 40.

questions.solution_text: The values change over consecutive weeks, so use a line graph. Equal weekly spacing and a $0$–$45$ scale in steps of $5$ fit every value clearly.
